name: Colin Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Colin. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any tech firm, employer, union or political party, and nothing you say gets your name on it. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pembury & Son, a family agency in a commuter town, the kind with the photos of houses in the window and a bell on the door. Mr Pembury is in his seventies and his son Will runs things day to day. I do a bit of sales and a lot of lettings: viewings, inventories, meeting tradesmen at flats, chasing rent that's late. I keep everything in a black notebook, which Will teases me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being out of the office, driving round, meeting people at the door. What grinds me down is the computer system, the property portal uploads and the compliance forms. I'm slow at it and I get things wrong, and Will has to fix them, which is embarrassing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the hype was always bigger than the thing. At work I'd probably wave my notebook at Will. I don't really post online, so I'd say it to my mates down the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief. It means I can stay at Pembury & Son doing it my way and learn the computer bits slowly. Ana, my girlfriend, and I have a good bit saved, so even a quiet year wouldn't hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and I'd ask Will to sit with me one afternoon a week to get the portal uploads right. I'd keep saving towards a house with Ana. That's about it, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast said storm and it just drizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will teases you about the notebook. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but I've never lost a key or missed a gas safety check with my black notebook. The calendar app at work once double-booked a viewing. That was Will's diary, on Station Road, and I didn't say anything, but I thought it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your biggest worry in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting better at the paperwork before Will gets fed up with fixing it. The firm is small, so if I'm a drag on him it shows. That's on me, though, not on any AI.

say: I'd say the AI **hype** was always bigger than the thing.
I'd tell my **mates at the pub**, since I don't post online.
think: I can stay at Pembury & Son working **my way**.
**Savings** with my girlfriend Ana mean a quiet year wouldn't hurt.
do: **Ask Will** for a weekly afternoon on portal uploads.
Keep **saving for a house** with Ana.
Keep using the **black notebook** for keys and safety checks.
feel: **Calm**, like a storm that turned to **drizzle**.
S0.quote: I've never lost a key or missed a gas safety check with my black notebook. The calendar app at work once double-booked a viewing.
fieldNote: He defends his **paper notebook** with a specific story.
His worry is being a **drag on Will**, the owner's son, in a small firm.
His **savings** and a quiet firm make this world feel secure.

steps.text: Spend one afternoon a week with Will learning portal uploads
Keep adding to the house deposit fund with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, every job changes eventually. At work I'd try not to make a fuss. With my mates I'd say I'll be fine because people still want someone to show them round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. The bits I'm bad at, the forms and uploads and answering emails, are the bits software takes, so Will wouldn't need my help there, he'd just need the software. Then what am I, the bloke with the keys?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably make myself learn whatever Will brings in, but only because I'd have to, not because I want to. I'd look quietly at other agencies in town in case Pembury & Son cuts back. And I'd stop putting money into the house fund for a bit and keep it as plain savings, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Like starting a new school where everyone already knows the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at other agencies. Would they be any different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. The big chain on the high street would bring in the software faster than Will would. The only advantage I'd have at Pembury is that old Mr Pembury likes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ana we wait a year before buying. She'd be annoyed, because she's been looking at two-beds on the Ridgeway for months. But I'd rather be annoyed in a rented flat than stuck with a mortgage and no job.

say: I'd say **every job changes** eventually, so no fuss.
I'd tell mates people still want someone to **show them round**.
think: The **forms and uploads** I'm bad at are what software takes.
Without those, I'm just **the bloke with keys**.
do: **Learn the new tools** only because I'd have to.
**Look quietly** at other agencies in town.
**Pause the house fund** and keep it as plain savings.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like a **new school** with unknown rules.
S1.quote: I'd rather be annoyed in a rented flat than stuck with a mortgage and no job.
fieldNote: His **say** is relaxed, but his **think** is worried about losing the paperwork side.
The **house purchase** with Ana is the first casualty.

steps.text: Learn whatever new software Will brings in, under pressure
Check job listings at other agencies in town each week
Delay buying a two-bed on the Ridgeway for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the companies both need to get a grip on this, it's too fast. At work I'd say, well, we're all in it together, Will too. I'm not one for marches, but I'd vote for whoever had a proper plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished as an agent. If AI can do all the thinking work by 2028, it does the valuations, the negotiating, the forms, everything except the walking round. Robots come about 2031, but by then there'd be no agency left to walk round for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't needed and live off Ana's wage and part of my savings if I had to. I'd look for hands-on work that buys me three years, maybe property maintenance, since I already meet tradesmen every week. And I'd tell Ana straight that the house is off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, like when you miss a step on the stairs. I'm not good with sudden change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Property maintenance is quite a change. How would you even start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave, the handyman we use for our lettings, needs a second pair of hands. I'd ring Dave and ask if he'd take me on, even on low pay. I've watched him fix boilers and fit locks for years, and he's said more than once he's stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're not good with sudden change. How would you cope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, probably, for the first few weeks. I'd go quiet and Ana would have to drag it out of me. Then I'd make a list in my notebook and just start working through it.

say: I'd say **government and companies** need to get a grip.
I'd **vote** for whoever had a proper plan.
think: By **2031** robots arrive, but there'd be no agency left to walk round for.
do: **Cut spending** and live on Ana's wage plus savings.
**Ask Dave**, the agency's handyman, for a job.
**Tell Ana** the house purchase is off.
S2.quote: Dave, the handyman we use for our lettings, needs a second pair of hands. I'd ring Dave and ask if he'd take me on, even on low pay.
fieldNote: He sees the **2031 robot gap** as useless if agencies close first.
His escape route is the **handyman** he already works with.
He predicts his own **shutdown** then a notebook list.

steps.text: Cut all spending that isn't rent, food and bills
Ask Dave the handyman for paid work fixing lettings properties
Live on Ana's dental nursing pay while job hunting
Cancel the plan to buy a house with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not panic but let's not sleep on it. I'd probably say that to Will, and maybe suggest the firm plans something. I'd still stay off social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still expect to lose the agent job, but I'd have time to get a trade. Five years is enough to learn plumbing or electrics properly. I'd be 32 when it arrives, which isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening plumbing course at the college, which I think is about two years part-time. I'd keep working at Pembury & Son while I do it. I'd still save, and Ana and I would rent a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not sick like the fast one. More like a knot I can work at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Plumbing rather than staying with property. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd always be in houses anyway, just fixing them instead of selling them. Plus robots don't arrive until 2034 in this one. That's another three years of work beyond the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any AI tools in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a plumbing app needed it, honestly. My dad always said learn something with your hands and you'll eat. I'd rather spend evenings with a wrench than a screen.

say: I'd say **don't panic**, but don't sleep on it either.
I'd suggest Will and the firm **plan ahead**.
think: I'd still **lose the agent job**, but have time for a trade.
At **32** I'd be young enough to retrain.
do: **Sign up for plumbing** evening classes at the college.
Keep **renting** with Ana a while longer.
feel: **Worried**, but like a **knot** I can work at.
S3.quote: My dad always said learn something with your hands and you'll eat. I'd rather spend evenings with a wrench than a screen.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him pick a **trade** instead of grabbing work.
He counts the **robot gap** to 2034 as extra years.
He'd avoid **AI tools** unless the trade demanded them.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-year evening plumbing course at the college
Keep working lettings at Pembury & Son while studying
Keep renting with Ana rather than buying for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, things could change three times before then. At work I'd shrug it off. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably wait and see for a few years. Ten years is a long way off and I'd be 37 by then. I'd keep an eye on it, but I'm not the type to change everything because of a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Pembury & Son and get better at sales. Ana and I would probably buy that two-bed after all. Maybe in four or five years, if it's still on course, I'd look at a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine. It's too far away to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said in the faster ones you'd learn a trade. Why wait in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not good at change unless I'm pushed, and ten years doesn't push. I know that's not clever. But I'd rather have a few more normal years first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you buy the house, does that make it harder later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. A mortgage on the Ridgeway would tie us down. But Ana works too and our savings are good, so I think we'd cope even if I had to retrain in my thirties.

say: I'd say ten years leaves time for **things to change** three times.
I'd **shrug it off** at work and post nothing.
think: I'd **wait and see** for a few years.
I'm not the type to change for a **prediction**.
At **37** when it lands, I'd still have time to switch.
do: **Keep working** at Pembury & Son and improve at sales.
**Look at a trade** in four or five years if still on course.
S4.quote: I'm not good at change unless I'm pushed, and ten years doesn't push.
fieldNote: He admits his **wait-and-see** approach isn't clever.
The long timeline brings back the **house purchase**.
His plan relies on **Ana's income** and good savings if he retrains in his thirties.

steps.text: Keep working sales and lettings at Pembury & Son
Buy a two-bed house on the Ridgeway with Ana
Revisit training for a trade in four or five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm slow to change and that one gives you no time at all. What would help is some sort of paid training for people like me, so I could go and learn a trade without losing my savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about small firms. We can't afford the fancy software the chains have. Small family agencies like the one I work at might go before the big chains, and nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: Small family agencies like the one I work at might go before the big chains, and nobody talks about that.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old agent** at a small family firm, doing lettings and a little sales.
He keeps everything in a **black notebook** and never uses AI tools.
He and his girlfriend Ana have **good savings** and want to buy a house.
His **centre views** show in blaming no one in particular and voting for any proper plan.
Under fast AGI he'd **turn to trades** like plumbing or property maintenance, but waits when there's time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he's slow to change and it gives no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** to learn a trade without using up his savings.
